newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH says DFS buy to lift profit.
newsitem.headline: LVMH says DFS buy to lift profit.

text.p: LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton group said on Wednesday that the planned acquisition of a 58.75 percent stake in U.S. duty-free goods group DFS would lift operating profit by about 30 percent and turnover by close to 50 percent.
DFS said on Tuesday that an outside arbitrator appointed by its shareholders had cleared the sale of a majority of the duty free chain to LVMH.

LVMH said in a statement that it would pay $2.47 billion, or 12.85 billion francs, for 58.75 percent of DFS, which generates $2.9 billion annually through sales at 180 outlets, concentrated mainly in the Pacific Rim countries.
"Thanks to this acquisition, the turnover of the LVMH group will increase close to 50 percent and the operating result around 30 percent," it said.
LVMH said it expected to acquire the majority holding once the deal is cleared by U.S. regulatory authorities. It has already filed for clearance with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.

LVMH said DFS's financial performance was exceptional -- it has an operating margin close to 15 percent, average return on equity of 85 percent in the past three years, and cash flow averaging $290 million annually over the past three years.
"The world's leading luxury goods group thus acquires the world's leading retailer of luxury goods," LVMH said.
LVMH said it was "committed to preserving the autonomy of DFS, whose previous strategy, the root of its remarkable success, will be pursued in its integrity, notably in relations with its suppliers".

In its statement issued in California, DFS said arbitrator Ira Millstein had cleared the deal "provided that the parties agree to certain conditions...These conditions include, among other things, a written agreement that must be signed by LVMH that would ensure the long-term autonomy of DFS and its management, address the potential concerns of DFS suppliers who are competitors of LVMH, and protect the rights of DFS's minority owners".

One of the DFS shareholders who had opposed the deal, Robert Miller, said the arbitrator's agreement appeared to have established strong protection for minority shareholders "and imposed stringent conditions on LVMH's ability to achieve synergies at the expense of DFS and its suppliers who compete directly with LVMH products".

Miller said in a separate statement that he and the other dissenting shareholder, Tony Pilaro, "will closely monitor LVMH's adherence to restrictions on integrating DFS into its operations. There are serious antitrust issues, and DFS suppliers have told us they are cooperating with the FTC as it reviews LVMH's recent Hart-Scott-Rodino filing".
Newspapers have reported that LVMH filed with the FTC last week and sought an expedition of the process, which normally takes a month. LVMH would only confirm that it had filed.

A spokeswoman for LVMH said the slight increase in the price -- 12.85 billion francs, up from 12.6 billion when the agreement was announced at the end of October -- reflects the rise in the dollar's value against the franc.
